title: The rope that wouldn't reach
hookLine: a mother tries to tie up her toddler, and every rope in the house comes up two fingers short
carry: bhakti: God can't be tied, except by love
tomorrow: jnana: salt in water, and 'you are that'
last: NOT WHETHER YOU'LL ACT, BUT HOW.

cards: A village of cowherds, on the banks of the Yamuna. A mother named Yashoda is churning butter, singing about her little boy. The boy is Krishna, still a toddler, and he's hungry, so he climbs into her lap to nurse.
Then the milk on the stove boils over. She sets him down and runs to it.
The toddler, furious at being put down, picks up a stone, cracks the pot of yogurt she was churning, and runs off to a corner, where he feeds the stolen butter to the monkeys.
Yashoda comes back, sees the mess, and picks up a stick.

teach.b: This is from the Bhagavata Purana, the great book of Krishna's life, in its tenth part. Yashoda chases him. He runs, looking back over his shoulder, eyes wide and frightened, a little actor.
She catches him, throws away the stick, and decides to tie him to a big wooden mortar so he'll stay out of trouble. The rope is too short, by two fingers' width. Another rope.
Still two fingers short. She brings every rope in the house, and the neighbors are laughing now. Every time, two fingers short.
Yashoda is sweating, her hair coming loose, flowers falling from it.
And Krishna, seeing how hard his mother is trying, lets himself be tied. Here's what devotees hear in it. In the Bhagavata, this child is God.
The text stops to say he has no inside and no outside, no before and no after. No amount of rope or effort can tie him.
But he allows himself to be bound by love. A popular devotional reading of the two fingers: one is our effort, the other is grace, and only when both are there does the rope reach.

teach.h: DAMODARA: A ROPE AROUND THE BELLY.
teach.b: The story gave Krishna the name Damodara: the one with a rope around his belly. On the bhakti road, God isn't only the king of the universe. He's also the child who wants butter, and lets his mother win.
It's why many Hindu homes offer butter and sugar to a little image of baby Krishna, Bal Gopal: love is the one rope that reaches him.

how: Vaishnava Hindus, especially in Gaudiya communities, celebrate the Damodara story in the month of Kartika, offering small lamps each evening and singing hymns to Krishna as Damodara; many families keep an image of baby Krishna, Bal Gopal, and offer him butter and sugar (makhan mishri).

o: action, like Yashoda's effort with the rope
fate that decides how a story will end
a kind of sacred rope used in a story

s: in the story, Yashoda ties Krishna up on her first try
every rope comes up two fingers short, until he lets himself be tied.
the story gives Krishna the name Damodara
dama, a rope, and udara, the belly.
the story comes from the Ramayana
it's from the Bhagavata Purana, the book of Krishna's life, in its tenth part.

games.q: you're Yashoda. every rope you bring is two fingers too short to tie your little boy. what happens?
o: you give up and let him run.
you keep trying until you're exhausted, and he lets himself be tied.
a neighbor ties him for you.
games.why: seeing her effort, Krishna lets himself be bound. devotees say he can't be tied by rope, only by love.

practice: Think of someone you love who is hard to hold on to, a child who runs, a friend far away, a parent getting older, and picture them clearly.

Effort alone can't tie them to you, so breathe in and let the love be there anyway, and breathe out and let go of the rope. If you pray, you can hold God this way too, as someone you love, near and a little mischievous.

wordCard.voice: Karma, action, is the word these weeks carry, and today's action belongs to Yashoda: all that effort, until love does the rest.

orig.note: Sanskrit: dama, a rope + udara, the belly. A name of Krishna from this story.

carryVoice: Hold on to this: bhakti. God can't be tied, except by love. Day three hundred three, done.
